Expected SARSA

SARSA's target depends on a random next action, which adds noise. Expected SARSA replaces that one sample with the average over all next actions, weighted by how likely the policy is to take each. Its updates have the same mean as SARSA's and less variance.

One transition on the cliff from Lesson 53: reward $R = -1$, $\gamma = 1$, and the agent lands in a cell on the cliff edge. Drag the action values at $S'$, set ε, and sample SARSA targets.

Step size on the cliff

Average reward per episode over the first 100 episodes of cliff walking, for each step size $\alpha$ ($\varepsilon = 0.1$, 15 runs each). S&B §6.6 plots the same comparison.

The cliff is deterministic, so once $S'$ is known the only randomness left in SARSA's target is $A'$. Expected SARSA removes it, so large steps do not make it jumpy and it keeps improving as $\alpha$ grows towards 1.

The maths

Expected SARSA's update:

$$Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \sum_a \pi(a \mid S_{t+1})\, Q(S_{t+1}, a) - Q(S_t, A_t)\Big]$$

The sum is the value of $S_{t+1}$ under the current $Q$ and the policy $\pi$, as in Lesson 23. With $\bar Q(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\,Q(s, a)$, SARSA's target averages to it:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\, Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) \,\big|\, S_{t+1}, R_{t+1}\big] = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, \bar Q(S_{t+1})$$

So the two methods move $Q$ the same way on average. The difference is the spread. Given $S_{t+1}$ and $R_{t+1}$, SARSA's target has variance

$$\gamma^2 \sum_a \pi(a \mid S_{t+1}) \big(Q(S_{t+1}, a) - \bar Q(S_{t+1})\big)^2$$

and Expected SARSA's has none. Variance from the environment (which $S_{t+1}$ and $R_{t+1}$ occur) is the same for both. The price is a sum over actions on every step.

Two special cases. If $\pi$ is greedy, the sum puts all its weight on the best action and the target is $R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a)$: Expected SARSA is Q-learning. And $\pi$ in the target need not be the policy the agent follows, so Expected SARSA can learn off-policy about any target policy, with Q-learning as the greedy case.

For ε-greedy with $|\mathcal{A}|$ actions and a unique greedy action $a^*$, the weights are

$$\pi(a^* \mid s) = 1 - \varepsilon + \frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{A}|}, \qquad \pi(a \mid s) = \frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{A}|} \ \ (a \ne a^*)$$
